analysis.one_liner: Restores victims' right to sue nuclear weapons contractors directly for radiation injuries, with the government guaranteeing payment.
analysis.headline: Backed by 40 senators — 31 Democrats and 9 Republicans — the bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee and was placed on the Senate calendar in October 1990, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 1984 law had made the federal government the only defendant — and a federal claims statute the only remedy — for people injured by radiation from atomic weapons testing run by private contractors. That shielded the contractors from direct lawsuits, jury trials, and the full range of damages. S. 982 would have repealed that shield, let victims sue the contractors directly, paused the legal filing deadlines that ran out while the old law was in force, and required the government to pay any judgments while reimbursing contractors for successful defense costs and settlements.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured, or whose family members were killed, by radiation from atomic weapons testing — downwinders, uranium workers, and test site workers whose lawsuits had been dismissed because the law forced them to sue the government instead of the contractors. They regain the right to a day in court with a jury and the full range of damages, deadlines that expired under the old law are paused, and the government guarantees the judgments will actually be paid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Radiation victims of nuclear weapons testing

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provision that substituted the United States as the defendant in every suit against private contractors for radiation injuries from atomic weapons testing, restoring the contractors' civil liability so victims can sue them in court.

Ends the rule making the Federal Tort Claims Act the sole remedy, which means victims are no longer limited to a no-jury claim against the government and can pursue ordinary civil suits against the companies that ran the testing.

Pauses the clock: the years the old law was in effect do not count toward any federal or state statute of limitations, and people whose earlier suits were dismissed under the old law can refile, with cases whose deadlines were about to expire getting a fresh one-year window.
Guarantees collection: the United States must indemnify and guarantee payment of any judgment for a claimant, so a courtroom win cannot be defeated by a contractor's inability to pay.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government — and ultimately taxpayers — which must pay any judgments awarded to victims and reimburse contractors for successful defense costs, attorney fees, and settlement amounts. Contractors face litigation and the exposure of a jury trial, but under the committee-approved version they are largely made financially whole by the indemnity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, plus litigation burdens on contractors

drawbacks.text: The cost lands on taxpayers twice over: the government pays the victims' judgments and also reimburses contractors for successful defense costs, fees, and good-faith settlements, which softens the financial consequences for the companies considerably.

The committee amendment caps attorney fees at ten percent of actual damages. That limits costs, but in complex radiation cases that stretch over years it could make it harder for some victims to find willing counsel.

Because contractors are reimbursed even when they lose, the bill's main leverage over the companies is the ordeal of litigation and jury exposure rather than money out of their own pockets — an honest supporter would concede it is a victim-compensation channel as much as a contractor-accountability measure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the victims themselves the gain is concrete: a path back into court after their suits were dismissed, deadlines restored, and a government guarantee that judgments are paid. The cost is real but diffuse — taxpayers fund both the judgments and the contractors' reimbursement, and the committee design means the companies bear little direct financial risk. The fee cap keeps the bill from becoming a windfall for lawyers. On balance the bill was a genuine remedy for a specific group of injured people, paid for by the Treasury rather than by the companies it re-exposed to suit.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee reported the bill favorably in October 1990 and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but the Senate never took it up for a vote before that Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Harry Reid of Nevada introduced the bill on May 12, 1989 with a large bipartisan list of original cosponsors, including Republicans Warner, Thurmond, Hatch, McCain, Garn, and Chafee — senators from states whose constituents were downwinders of the Nevada Test Site.
The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Courts and Administrative Practice Subcommittee, which held hearings in August 1989 and approved it favorably without amendment on March 1, 1990.

On October 11, 1990 the full Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment, and on October 16, 1990 Senator Biden reported it to the Senate; the amendment capped attorney fees at ten percent and added the government indemnity and contractor reimbursement provisions.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 986) on October 16, 1990, but no floor vote ever came, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The government contractors whose radiation-injury liability the 1984 law had absorbed — and the Treasury, which did not have to take on guaranteed judgments and contractor reimbursements. Radiation victims got nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nuclear contractors kept their court shield

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily bipartisan: 31 of 55 Democrats and 9 of 45 Republicans cosponsored, and the bill cleared the Democratic-led Judiciary Committee; it died for lack of floor time, not a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill strips these contractors of the 1984 arrangement that made the federal government the sole defendant in radiation-injury suits, re-exposing them to direct lawsuits, jury trials, and the full range of damages. The committee amendment blunts the blow: the government must reimburse them for successful defense costs and settlements and guarantee payment of judgments.
The bill opens a new field of litigation against the contractors, but the committee amendment caps fees at ten percent of actual damages, limiting what these lawyers can collect.
